blocks.text: That the Egyptians too held the same view is shown by these words of Diodorus in book 1: Τὸν δ᾽ ἀετὸν Θηβαῖοι τιμῶσι, διὰ τὸ βασιλικὸν εἶναι δοκεῖν τοῦτο ζῶον, καὶ τοῦ Διὸς ἄξιον [Ton d᾽ aeton Thēbaioi timōsi, dia to basilikon einai dokein touto zōon, kai tou Dios axion]· The Thebans worship the eagle, because they think this animal is royal and worthy of Jupiter. From there the cult of the eagle had also spread to the Arabs. The Talmudists, in the treatise On Idolatry, ch. 1, fol. 11 b: בתי ע״ז קבועין אלו הן בית בל בבבל בית נבו בכורסי תרעתא שבמפג צריפא שבאשקלון נשרא שבערביא, These are the fixed idolatrous [II, 741] temples: the temple of Bel at Babylon, the temple of Nebo at Borsippa, Atergatis at Hierapolis, Venus Urania at Ascalon, and the Eagle in Arabia. Those temples are called fixed whose idols are worshipped on every day of the year, as the Gloss explains. Thus Bel was worshipped at Babylon and Nebo at Borsippa (for instead of בכורסי read בבורסיף). And at Hierapolis Derceto, or Atergatis, whose worship at Hierapolis Lucian describes at length in his book On the Syrian Goddess. Derceto, or Atergatis, is in Hebrew תרעתא Tirgata. And Hierapolis is ממבג Mambeg, as in Arabic منبج [Manbij] Manbeg. In Pliny too the text once read Bambyca and Mambeg, which was altered into Magog. Accordingly in the Talmud one should read שבממבג instead of שבמפג. Further, we know from Herodotus that Venus Urania was held in the highest worship at Ascalon. Hence she seems to be the צריפא שבאשקלון, Tseripha, which is at Ascalon. Why she is called צריפא Tseripha, however, is not quite clear. Unless you think she was named from casting [metal]; for among the Hebrews צרף tsaraph means to cast. Hence the Talmudists' בית נצרפי, house of molten images, that is, a temple of idols. Or from lust, over which she presides. For in Arabic صرف [ṣarafa] tsarapha means to burn with lust, and صارفة [ṣārifa] tsaripha is said of a female dog when she is in heat and burns with lust for the male. It remains for us to speak of the eagle of the Arabs. It was the idol of the Dulkelaites among the Homerites, a very well-known people of Arabia Felix. Alcamus: النسر الصنم كان لذي الكلا بارض حمير [al-nasr al-ṣanam kāna li-Dhī al-Kalāʿ bi-arḍ Ḥimyar] The Eagle was the idol of Dulkela in the land of Humeir, that is, of the Homerites. Evidently among the Arabs too this opinion had prevailed, that the eagle is the chief of the birds. So Muaphius, in the book entitled نفحات الازهار [Nafaḥāt al-azhār] Fragrances of Flowers, attributes this to the impure Muhammad: هبط علي جبرييل فقال يا محمد ان لكل شي سيد فسيد البشر ادم وسيد ولد ادم انت وسيد الروم صحيب وسيد فارس سليمان وسيد [col. 164] الحبش بلال وسيد الشجر السدر وسيد الطير النسر [habaṭa ʿalayya Jabrīl fa-qāla yā Muḥammad inna li-kull shayʾ sayyid fa-sayyid al-bashar Ādam wa-sayyid walad Ādam anta wa-sayyid al-Rūm Ṣuhayb wa-sayyid Fāris Salmān wa-sayyid al-Ḥabash Bilāl wa-sayyid al-shajar al-sidr wa-sayyid al-ṭayr al-nasr] Gabriel came down to me and said: O Muhammad, every thing has its lord. The lord of men was Adam; but you are the lord of the sons of Adam. And the lord of the Greeks is Sahib, and of the Persians Soliman, and of the Abyssinians Bilal. And of trees the connarus, a species of lotus, and of birds the eagle, etc. Now, if one wishes to hear the Hebrews: Josephus, On the Jewish War, book 3, chapter 5, writes that the Romans had the eagle as the standard in the first cohort of the legion because the ἀετὸς [aetos] is βασιλεύς τε οἰωνῶν ἁπάντων, καὶ ἀλκιμώτατος [basileus te oiōnōn hapantōn, kai alkimōtatos], king of all birds, and the strongest. And Kimchi on Ezech. XVII, 3.: הנשר הוא משל לנבוכדנצר מלך בבל כי הנשר מלך העופות וכן נבוכדנצר היה מלך על כל מלכי הארץ, The eagle there is a figure of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, because, as the eagle is king of the birds, so [II, 742] Nebuchadnezzar was king over all the kings of the earth. Hence in the Masal Kadmoni the thirty-eighth Fable bears this title:
צורת הנשר על מושבו : וסנהדרי׳ העוף יושבים סביבו :
